articles.title: Sony makes bold claim about game ownership
articles.summary: Sony's argument about software ownership is a strange reductio ad absurdum that attempts to prove the opposite of what is actually true. The idea that gamers don't own what they pay for, but rather have a limited right to use it, is a common misconception. In reality, software is sold as copies, not as a singular entity, and its value is determined by its ability to be used. This is evident in the example of Resident Evil Requiem, where the game's value is not tied to a single copy, but rather to the ability to play it. The proposed law that Sony is proposing, which would require vendors to provide service for a reasonable period after purchase or refund unused value to the purchaser, is a necessary step to protect consumers from being left with unplayable software.

articles.title: .name Termination
articles.summary: Nearly twenty-five years ago, I registered neil.fraser.name to provide a stable presence on the Internet. The website, email address, and server for APIs were all registered under this domain. Verisign proposed the destruction of the 3rd level of the '.name' hierarchy in 2026, which was approved by ICANN. The 3rd level is unique to '.name' and has a full whois record, unlike third-level domains sold by shady operators. The website and email address will vanish in February, and IoT devices linked to the domain will become available for registration, potentially allowing unauthorized access and control.

articles.title: You Don't Need Initial-Scale In Your HTML
articles.summary: The viewport meta tag is a crucial element in modern HTML, allowing websites to scale nicely on various devices. Introduced by Apple in 2007, it enables sites to load full desktop versions on small screens, reducing zooming and panning issues. While the initial-scale attribute was once necessary, it's now largely obsolete, as modern browsers handle the scaling automatically. By including the viewport meta tag, developers can simplify their code and reduce unnecessary work, saving 19 bytes.

articles.title: How Swiss Tables Work in Go’s Built-in Map
articles.summary: Swiss Tables are a new design for Go's built-in map, replacing the old runtime implementation. This design is based on the concept of a table, where each row represents a key-value pair. The table is divided into two parts: the row keys and the column keys. The row keys are used to store the key-value pairs, while the column keys are used to access the values. This design is more efficient than the old implementation, as it allows for faster lookup and insertion of key-value pairs. The new design also provides better support for large datasets, as it can handle a large number of key-value pairs without needing to grow the underlying storage.

articles.title: The Browser's Main Thread Is Expensive
articles.summary: The browser's main thread is expensive due to its heavy workload of running JavaScript, event handlers, timers, network response callbacks, and the framework's internals, which all execute in a seemingly unrelated order to screen refresh cycles. This expensive resource handling can cause stuttering, button delays, and other jank issues, even if the code itself is not slow. To handle this, developers can split tasks into two categories: running JavaScript and drawing the screen, and use techniques like requestAnimationFrame, style calculation, layout, and paint to optimize performance.
